title: Detection and quantitation of small proteins using mass spectrometry
projectDescription: Small proteins or microproteins, despite long being ignored, have important roles in the regulation of larger protein complexes, metabolic pathways and gene expression. However, these proteins remain underrepresented in proteomics studies due to low detection efficiency in traditional mass spectrometry workflows. Their inherent characteristics often lead to depletion during sample preparation and a low detection efficiency in liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). To improve detection and quantitation, we took advantage of the large set of documented small proteins in Escherichia coli and systematically compared and optimized different sample preparation and LC-MS approaches. We evaluated different top-down and bottom-up approaches, including data-dependent acquisition (DDA), data-independent acquisition (DIA) and parallel reaction monitoring (PRM). Our data highlight the benefit of top-down proteomics for identifying new small proteins and bottom-up preparation coupled with PRM acquisition for quantitation of protein levels in different growth conditions. Our systematic comparison can serve as a guideline for MS detection of small proteins in all organisms.
sampleProcessingProtocol: E. coli cell pellets were digested in three different approaches. In the SPEED protocol, cells were mixed (1:5) with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and incubated for 5 minutes before neutralization with 2 M Tris.HCl-buffer (pH 10.5). For the in-solution digest, they were mixed in the same ratio with UA20 buffer (6M Urea in 80% MS-grade water and 20% ACN), supplemented with protease inhibitors (Sigma-Aldrich, CAT#04693124001) and subjected to cell lysis using a rod sonifier for three cycles of 30 s on 30% power, 50% duty cycle and 30 sec cooling on ice. For the S-Trap protocol pellets were mixed with of lysis buffer (10% SDS, 100 mM TEAB pH 8.5), supplemented with protease inhibitors and subjected to the same cell lysis using a rod sonifier. Samples were then cleared from cell debris by centrifugation (500g, 5 min). The supernatants were collected and reduced by addition of 4 µl TCEP for 30 min at 37°C with mild agitation, followed by alkylation with 8 µl IAA for 30 min in the dark with mild agitation. For the SPEED protocol, pH was adjusted to neutrality with 1% TFA and MS-grade Trypsin was added in an enzyme to protein ratio 1:50 using 100 µl digestion buffer (50mM ammonium bicarbonate (ABC), pH 8,5). For the in-solution workflow, trypsin in the same ratio was added using 488 µl digestion buffer (50mM ABC, pH 8.5). In the S-Trap, the samples were acidified with 12 µl 12% phosphoric acid, diluted with 750 µl of the S-Trap binding buffer (1 M TEAB Buffer and Methanol (10:90)) and transferred to S-Trap mini columns (Protifi). SDS removal was conducted by three washing cycles with 400 µl S-Trap binding buffer prior to digestion. Trypsin was added in an enzyme to protein ratio 1:50 using 125 µl digestion buffer (50mM ABC, pH 8.5). For all workflows, the digested peptides were diluted 1:1 with 0.1% TFA and desalted with C18-SPE cartridges (25 mg, Biotage). After equilibration with 2 mL acetonitrile (ACN), 1 mL 50% ACN/1% acetic acid and 2 mL 0.1% TFA the samples were loaded onto the cartridge, washed with 2 mL 0,1% TFA and eluted with 1 mL 80% ACN/0,1% TFA. The eluted fractions were dried using an Eppendorf concentrator and stored at -20°C. Samples were reconstituted in 5% ACN with 0.1% formic acid (FA), loaded onto an Acclaim PepMap C18 capillary trapping column (particle size 3 µm, L = 20 mm) and trapped for 6 min with a flow rate of 6 μL/min using a loading buffer composed of 0.05% TFA in H2O. Separation was carried out on a ReproSil C18-PepSep analytical column (particle size = 1.9 µm, ID = 75 µm, L = 25 cm, Bruker Corporation, Billerica, USA) using a nano-HPLC (Dionex U3000 RSLCnano) at a temperature of 55 °C. For top-down LC-MS, Proteins were separated by a gradient of buffer A (100% H2O and 0.1% FA) and B (80% ACN, 20% H2O, and 0.1% FA) with a constant flow rate of 400 nL/min. The gradient went from 4% to 33% buffer B in 75 min, 33-65% B in 15 min, 65-95% B in 1 min followed by constant flow at 95% B for 11 min. Eluate was analyzed in data-dependent mode employing splitted MS1 windows for precursor selection as well as a modified BoxCar as described by Meier-Credo et al. (2023) on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer coupled to the nano-HPLC by a Nano Flex ESI source. The gradient for bottom-up LC-MS went from 4% to 48% buffer B in 90 min. For data-dependent acquisition, MS1 survey scans were acquired over a scan range of 350–1400 m/z in the Orbitrap detector (resolution = 120k, automatic gain control (AGC) = 2e5, and maximum injection time: 50 ms). Sequence information was acquired by a “ddMS2 OT HCD” MS2 method with a fixed cycle time of 5 s for MS/MS scans. MS2 scans were generated from the most abundant precursors with a minimum intensity of 3e4 and charge states from two to five. Selected precursors were isolated in the quadrupole using a 1.4 Da window and HCD fragmented at 30 % normalized collision energy. For Orbitrap MS2, an AGC of 5e4 with dynamic maximum injection time were used (resolution = 30k). Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s with a mass tolerance of 10 ppm. Peptides were also analysed in data-independent acquisition mode on the same instrument. MS1 survey scans were acquired over a scan range of 350 – 1650 Th in the Orbitrap detector (resolution = 120k, AGC = 5e5, and maximum injection time: 100 ms). Sequence information was acquired by a tMS2 method with the following settings. MS2 scans were generated in a scan range of 350 – 2000 Th with isolation windows proposed by Muntel et al. (2019). Fragmentation was induced by HCD at 27% normalized collision energy. For Orbitrap MS2, an AGC of 1e6 with dynamic injection time and a minimum of 6 desired points per peak (resolution = 30k). The analysis in parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) mode was acquired using the “tMS2 OT HCD” MS2 method. Targets were isolated in the quadrupole with a window of 1.6 Th for fragmentation induced by HCD at 27 % normalized collision energy. MS2 spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap (resolution = 15k, AGC = 2e5).
dataProcessingProtocol: MS raw data were matched against a FASTA file downloaded from UniProtKB (May 2024) for E. coli K-12 (UP000000625) using different software according to the type of data acquired in the mass spectrometer. For all database searches, a minimum of one unique peptide was set as a requirement for protein identification. To compare the search tools in an unbiased manner, we kept most settings unchanged, only selecting relevant PTM’s and changing the minimum number of amino acids in identified peptides from seven to six. In all searches, a false discovery rate of 1% was applied at all levels. For all bottom-up searches, carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues was set as a static modification, and acetylation on the protein N-terminus and oxidation of methionine residues were included as variable modifications. For FragPipe top-down searches, the 22.0 version was used applying the nonspecific-peptidome workflow. Default settings were employed allowing peptides of 7 - 65 amino acids and nonspecific digestion. No changes were made on precursor mass tolerance (40 ppm) and fragment ion tolerance (7 ppm). Acetylation on the protein N-terminus and oxidation of methionine residues were included as variable modifications. For PEAKS top-down searches, the 10.6 version was used applying the unspecific digestion settings. No changes were made on precursor mass tolerance (15 ppm) and fragment ion tolerance (0.02 Da). A maximum of 3 variable PTM’s were allowed per peptide. For MaxQuant DDA searches, version 2.5.2.0 was used with the following settings. Minimum tryptic peptide length of six amino acids and a maximum of two missed cleavage sites. According to the standard settings, precursor mass tolerance was set to 4.5 ppm and fragment ion tolerance to 20 ppm. For FragPipe DDA searches, version 22.0 was used with the following settings. Minimum peptide length of six amino acids and a maximum of two missed cleavage sites, considering semi specific digestion. According to the standard settings, precursor and fragment ion mass tolerances were set to 20 ppm. For PEAKS DDA searches, version 10.6 was used with standard settings in the semi specific digest mode. No changes were made on precursor mass tolerance (15 ppm) and fragment ion tolerance (0.02 Da). A maximum of 3 variable PTM’s were allowed per peptide.  For DIA-NN DIA searches, version 1.9 was used with the following settings. Library-free search was conducted with tryptic peptide lengths of 6 – 30 amino acids and a maximum of two missed cleavage sites. Precursors charges of 1 – 6 and precursor m/z set from 300 to 1800. Matching between runs was enabled with heuristic protein inference. The raw report.tsv output file was analysed in R using the r/diann package and the data was filtered for proteotypicity, and a 1% FDR cut-off on the Q.Value, PG.Q.Value, Lib.Q.Value and Lib.PG.Q.Value, following the instructions from the developers. For PEAKS DIA searches, version 10.6 was used with standard settings in the semi specific digest mode. No changes were made on precursor mass tolerance (15 ppm) and fragment ion tolerance (0.02 Da). A maximum of 3 variable PTM’s were allowed per peptide. For FragPipe DIA searches, version 22.0 was used with the default workflows DIA_DIA-Umpire_SpecLib_Quant and DIA_SpecLib_Quant. For both workflows, a minimum peptide length of six amino acids and a maximum of two missed cleavage sites was employed. Precursor and fragment ion mass tolerances were set to 20 ppm. For Spectronaut DIA searches, version 19.0 was used in directDIA mode. Peptides with up to 2 miscleavages were allowed in the search settings with N-terminal methionine stripping activated. To identify potential modifications in peptides deriving from small proteins we ran open searches using the “Open” default workflow from FragPipe in version 22.0 in our DDA dataset. Precursor mass tolerance was set to a window of -150 to 700 Da to cover mass shifts deriving from PTMs, losses, and mutations. Fragment mass tolerance was set to 20 ppm. Protein digestion was selected as nonspecific with peptide length range from 6 to 50 aa or 500 to 10000 Da. Up to two miscleavages were tolerated. MSFragger was set with localization-aware open search (LOS) algorithm, with deisotoping, mass calibration, parameter optimization, and monoisotopic correction enabled. PTM-Shepherd was used for mass shift summarization.
